paras: The expulsion of Black railroad workers near Pennington Gap was the forcing out of about 100 Black laborers from a railroad construction camp in Lee County, Virginia, by armed white men from Harlan County, Kentucky, in August 1903. The workers left after a display of firearms, and work at the camp was reported suspended. A short wire account ran in Virginia and New York papers, and both an Arizona daily and the St. Paul Appeal cited the episode as mob violence used to drive men from their work.
The camp housed workers on a branch of the Louisville and Nashville railroad near Pennington Gap, and its contractors employed about 100 Black men.

According to the dispatch, a "large crowd" of white men from Harlan County, "heavily armed with Winchester[s]", entered the camp and demanded that the contractors at once discharge the Black workers. When the contractors refused, the men went to the workers themselves and ordered them to leave the works and "the country." Only a few of the workers resisted, and a display of firearms, in the dispatch's words, "had the desired effect."
Afterward no Black worker could be found in the vicinity. The Free Lance reported work "practically suspended," while the Sun said simply that work was suspended. No deaths or injuries were reported.
The coverage names none of the contractors, workers or armed men, and no report of arrests, prosecution or the workers' return was found.

White papers carried the episode as a brief wire item without comment. The Free Lance of Fredericksburg headed it "NEGROES ORDERED AWAY" over "A Mob Breaks up Construction Camp in Lee County," and the New York Sun ran it on August 12 as "RAN THE NEGROES OUT" over "Mob of Armed Whites Causes a Railroad Camp to Become Depopulated." Both called the men a "mob" but gave no reason for their demand.

Comment came from farther away. On August 20 the Bisbee Daily Review in Arizona wrote that when a mob demanded that Black workers quit, "the spirit of Judge Lynch is extended to driving men not from crime but from honest labor." The Deming Graphic in New Mexico reprinted the sentence on August 26 in a column of clipped paragraphs.

In the Black press, the St. Paul Appeal took up the episode in its editorial column of August 15. Answering Southern papers that "claimed that no Afro-Americans are prevented from earning a living by the labor of their hands," the Appeal pointed to "a mob of drunken Caucasians" that had acted a few days earlier against men "working on a rail road in Virginia." Only the Appeal described the attackers as drunken, and it set the item among paragraphs on lynching and British comment on President Roosevelt's letter to Governor Durbin.

The two news texts differ on the date. The Free Lance, dated Tuesday, August 11, placed the event on "Saturday," August 8, while the Sun's Norfolk dispatch, dated August 11, said "yesterday," or August 10. The texts are otherwise nearly word for word the same and appear to come from one report, so neither date is clearly better supported.

reader.title: Expulsion of Black railroad workers near Pennington Gap, Virginia
bases: Armed white men forced a railroad contractor's whole Black workforce to quit work and leave the area, an expulsion of workers from a job site (A1, A2).
A1 and A2 print nearly word-for-word the same dispatch, so they are one report; A4 and A5 are later comments that add no independent detail, and no report denies the event.

accounts.label: Wire report
accounts.gist: Heavily armed white men from Harlan County, Ky., entered the L&N camp near Pennington Gap, demanded the discharge of 100 Black workers, and when the contractors refused, ordered the workers out; a display of firearms ended resistance and work stopped.

accounts.label: Black editorial
accounts.gist: The St. Paul Appeal described the attackers as 'a mob of drunken Caucasians' acting against Afro-Americans working on a Virginia railroad, as proof that Black men were being kept from earning a living.

accounts.label: White editorial comment
accounts.gist: The Bisbee Daily Review said such a mob extended 'the spirit of Judge Lynch' to driving men from honest labor.

framing.detail: The Free Lance headed the item 'NEGROES ORDERED AWAY. A Mob Breaks up Construction Camp in Lee County.' and printed it without comment.
The New York Sun ran the Norfolk dispatch as 'RAN THE NEGROES OUT. Mob of Armed Whites Causes a Railroad Camp to Become Depopulated.'
The Bisbee Daily Review said the mob drove men 'not from crime but from honest labor', likening it to lynching; the Deming Graphic reprinted the line.
The St. Paul Appeal's editorial column used the 'mob of drunken Caucasians' in Virginia to rebut Southern papers' claim that Afro-Americans were free to earn a living.
